source_text: Deus igitur machinator constitutorque rerum, sicut in se- s cundo libro diximus, antequam praeclarum hoc opus mundi adoriretur, sanctum et incorruptibilem spiritum genuit, quem filium nuncuparet. et quamuis alios postea innumerabiles creauisset, quos angelos dicimus, hunc tamen solum primogenitum diuini nominis appellatione dignatus est, patria scilicet uirtute ac maiestate pollentem. esse autem summi dei filium, qui sit potestate maxima praeditus, non tantum congruentes in unum uoces prophetarum, sed etiam Trismegisti praedicatio et Sibyllarum uaticinia demonstrant. Hermes in eo libro qui λόγος τέλειος inscribitur, his usus est uerbis: ὁ κύριος καὶ τῶν πάντων ποιητὴς, ὃν Θεὸν καλεῖν νενομίκαμεν, ἐπεὶ τὸν δεύτερον ἐποίησε θεὸν ὁρατὸν καὶ αἰσθητὸν — αἰσθητὸν δέ φημι οὐ διὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι αὐτὸν, περὶ γὰρ τούτου, πότερον αὐτὸς αἰσθάνεται ἣ μή, εἰσαῦθις ῥηθήσεται, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι εἰς αἴσθησιν ὑποπέμπει καὶ εἰς ὅρασιν — ἐπεὶ οὖν τοῦτον ἐποίησε πρῶτον καὶ μόνον καὶ ἕνα, καλὸς δέ αὐτῷ ἐφάνη, καὶ πληρέστατος πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἠγάσθη τε καὶ πάνυ ἐφίλησεν ὤς ἴδιον τόκον. Sibylla Erythraea in carminis sui Et rursus in fine eiusdem carminis: principio, quod a summo deo exorsa est, filium dei ducem et imperatorem omnium his uersibus praedicat: παντοτρόφον κτίστην, ὅστις γλυκὺ πνεῦμα ἅπασιν κάτθετο, χἠγητῆρα Θεὸν πάντων ἐποίησεν. et rursus in fine: ἄλλον ἔδωκε Θεὸς πιστοῖς ἀνδράσσι γεραίρειν. et alia Sibylla praecipit hunc oportere cognosci: αὐτὸν σου γίνωσκε Θεὸν Θεοῦ υἱὸν ἐόντα. uidelicet et ipse est dei filius, qui per Solomonem sapientissimum regem diuino spiritu plenum locutus est ea quae subiecimus: dominus condidit me initium uiarum suarum in opera sua, ante saeculum fundauit me: in principio antequam terram faceret et antequam abyssos constitueret, priusquam procederent fontes aquarum, ante omnes colles genuit me. dominus fecit regiones et fines inhabitabiles sub caelo. cum pararet caelum, aderam illi, etcum secerneret suam sedem: cum super uentos faceret ualidas nubes et cum confirmatos ponebat fontes sub caelo, quando fortia faciebat fundamenta terrae, eram penes illum disponens. ego eram cui adgaudebat. cottidie autem iucundabar ante faciem eius, cum laetaretur orbe perfecto. idcirco illum Trismegistus δημιουργὸν TOO seou et Sibylla σύμβουλον appellat, quod tanta sapientia et uirtute sit instructus a deo patre, ut consilio eius et manibus uteretur in fabricatione mundi.
pass_a_gloss: God therefore, the contriver and establisher of things, as we said in the second book, before this glorious work of the world was begun, generated a holy and incorruptible Spirit, whom He called Son. And although He afterwards created innumerable others, whom we call angels, He nevertheless deemed this one alone, the firstborn, worthy of the divine name, clearly because He was powerful with paternal virtue and majesty. That He is the Son of the highest God, who is endowed with the greatest power, is demonstrated not only by the congruent voices of the prophets, but also by the prediction of Trismegistus and the prophecies of the Sibyls. Hermes, in that book which is inscribed Logos Teleios, used these words: The Lord and maker of all things, whom we are accustomed to call God, since He made a second God visible and perceptible - I say perceptible not because He perceives, for it will be said again whether He perceives or not, but because He sends into perception and into sight - since therefore He made this one first and only and alone, and He seemed good to Him and full of all good things, He delighted in Him and loved Him exceedingly as His own offspring. The Erythraean Sibyl, in her song, and again at the end of the same song, predicts the Son of God, the leader and commander of all, in these verses: the all-nourishing creator, who poured out sweet spirit to all, and made God the leader of all. And again at the end: God gave another to faithful men to reverence. And another Sibyl commands that this one ought to be recognized: know Him as God, the Son of God being. Clearly, He Himself is the Son of God, who spoke through Solomon, the wisest king, full of the divine Spirit, the things which we have subjoined: The Lord founded me in the beginning of His ways, in His works, before the century He established me; in the beginning, before He made the earth and before He established the abysses, before the springs of waters proceeded, before all the hills He generated me. The Lord made the regions and the uninhabitable boundaries under the heaven. When He was preparing the heaven, I was with Him; when He was separating His seat, when He was making strong clouds over the winds, and when He was setting the confirmed springs under the heaven, when He was making the strong foundations of the earth, I was with Him, arranging. I was the one in whom He delighted. Daily, however, I was rejoicing before His face, when He was rejoicing in the perfect orb. Therefore, Trismegistus calls Him the Demiurge, and the Sibyl calls Him the Counselor, because He is instructed with such wisdom and virtue by God the Father, that He uses His counsel and hands in the fabrication of the world.

bible_refs.note: The Lord founded me in the beginning of His ways

pass_b_english: As we discussed in our second book, God, the mastermind and creator of all things, brought into being a holy and incorruptible Spirit before He began His magnificent work of creating the world. This Spirit, whom God called His Son, was deemed worthy of the divine name - a distinction that set Him apart from the countless angels God would later create. The reason for this special status is clear: the Son possessed the same virtue and majesty as God the Father. The fact that the Son is the Son of the highest God, endowed with the greatest power, is a truth that emerges not only from the consistent testimony of the prophets but also from the writings of Trismegistus and the prophecies of the Sibyls. In his book, Logos Teleios, Hermes describes God as the Lord and maker of all things, who created a second, visible, and perceptible God - not because this second God perceives the world around Him, but because He makes the world perceptible to us. According to Hermes, God created this second God first and alone, and He was pleased with Him, seeing Him as full of all good things. As a result, God delighted in His Son and loved Him exceedingly, like a parent loves their child. The Erythraean Sibyl, in her song, predicts the coming of the Son of God, the leader and commander of all, describing Him as the all-nourishing creator who pours out His sweet Spirit to all and makes God the leader of all. She also writes that God gave another, the Son, to faithful people to reverence. Another Sibyl commands us to recognize the Son of God, saying, 'Know Him as God, the Son of God.' This Son of God, speaking through Solomon, the wisest king, who was filled with the divine Spirit, says, 'The Lord founded me in the beginning of His ways, in His works, before the century He established me; in the beginning, before He made the earth and before He established the abysses, before the springs of waters proceeded, before all the hills He generated me' (Proverbs 8:22-31). The Son continues, describing His role in creation, 'The Lord made the regions and the uninhabitable boundaries under the heaven. When He was preparing the heaven, I was with Him; when He was separating His seat, when He was making strong clouds over the winds, and when He was setting the confirmed springs under the heaven, when He was making the strong foundations of the earth, I was with Him, arranging.' The Son says, 'I was the one in whom He delighted. Daily, however, I was rejoicing before His face, when He was rejoicing in the perfect orb.' It is because the Son is endowed with such wisdom and virtue by God the Father that Trismegistus calls Him the Demiurge, and the Sibyl calls Him the Counselor, for He uses His counsel and hands in the fabrication of the world.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text and the embedded Greek quotations. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the required scripture citation (Proverbs 8:22-31) for the Solomon passage, which is an improvement over the gloss. The distinction regarding 'perceptible' (αἰσθητὸν) is handled correctly in both passes.
